chemicals.concentration_notes: Pennyroyal is distinctly noted as being "highly toxic" compared to other, milder garden mints47. Additionally, the risk is heavily dependent on concentration; extracted essential oils are far more potent and dangerous than the raw plant.
chemicals.description: Cats lack the specific liver enzymes required to properly break down and metabolize these plant essential oils23. Because the cat's body cannot process them, the compounds accumulate and cause systemic poisoning.
chemicals.name: Essential oils. The sources specifically identify pulegone and menthol as the toxic essential oil compounds found within the mint family

description:
Pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium) is a member of the mint family that is highly toxic to cats. It is much more dangerous than common peppermint. The plant contains a chemical called pulegone, which the cat's liver turns into a toxic substance that causes severe liver damage and can be fatal.

In the past, pennyroyal oil was sometimes used as a natural flea treatment, but this is extremely unsafe for cats. Even a small amount of the concentrated oil absorbed through the skin or swallowed can cause the liver to fail. Symptoms include vomiting, diarrhea, yellowing of the eyes or skin (jaundice), tremors, and collapse.

Eating the fresh plant is also a serious concern. If you suspect your cat has eaten pennyroyal or has come into contact with pennyroyal oil, this is an emergency. Please contact a veterinarian or an emergency animal hospital immediately.
emergencyNote: Gastrointestinal Decontamination (Emesis induction, Gastric Lavage, and Activated Charcoal)
name: Pennyroyal
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: pulegone (primary); metabolised to menthofuran in the liver — the true hepatotoxic agent
Mechanism: menthofuran causes direct hepatocellular necrosis (liver cell death); glutathione depletion amplifies the damage
Symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy; severe cases cause acute liver failure with jaundice, tremors, seizures, and collapse
Pennyroyal essential oil is especially dangerous — do NOT use it as a flea treatment; even topical application can cause fatal liver failure
Any exposure to pennyroyal oil is a veterinary emergency; plant ingestion also warrants prompt vet evaluation

symptoms.name: Liver damage progressing to liver failure
symptoms.notes: Unlike common garden mints (like spearmint or peppermint) that primarily irritate the digestive tract, Pennyroyal is explicitly noted for its severe systemic toxicity that attacks the cat's liver, which can ultimately lead to death.

symptoms.name: Seizures, tremors, uncoordinated gait, weakness, and lethargy
symptoms.notes: Seizures and profound neurological depression are hallmarks of severe mint/essential oil toxicity and are specifically associated with highly toxic mint plants like Pennyroyal.

symptoms.name: Vomiting, diarrhea, excessive drooling, loss of appetite, and difficulty swallowing
symptoms.notes: The essential oils in the mint family are highly irritating to a cat's gastrointestinal tract36. With Pennyroyal, these symptoms may occur alongside or precede more severe systemic organ failure.

symptoms.name: Difficulty breathing, coughing, and sneezing
symptoms.notes: In severe cases, the ingestion or inhalation of the essential oils found within toxic mint plants can cause significant respiratory distress45. Note: The provided sources do not specify the exact hourly onset times for these symptoms.

treatments.description: To prevent the highly toxic essential oils and plant material from being fully digested and absorbed into the bloodstream, the veterinarian will remove the stomach contents. This is achieved by medically inducing vomiting or, in extreme cases, performing a gastric lavage (stomach pump).
treatments.name: Gastrointestinal Decontamination (Emesis induction, Gastric Lavage, and Activated Charcoal)
treatments.notes: You should never attempt to induce vomiting at home (such as by giving the cat hydrogen peroxide or salt). There are no safe over-the-counter products for inducing vomiting in cats, and doing it yourself can cause significant injury, aspiration, or worsen the poisoning23. This procedure must be done.

treatments.description: The veterinarian will administer IV fluids to rehydrate the cat (especially if they have suffered from excessive vomiting and diarrhea), stabilize their system, and help support the body's organs as they process the toxins.
treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) Fluid Therapy and Hospitalization
treatments.notes: Unlike common garden mints that may only cause mild stomach upset, Pennyroyal is highly toxic and is specifically known to cause severe, potentially fatal liver damage and failure4. Due to the severe nature of Pennyroyal poisoning, the cat will require hospitalization alongside the fluid therapy.

treatments.description: The vet will administer specific supportive medications to manage the cat's clinical symptoms. This typically includes anti-nausea injections to stop active vomiting and antacids or gastric protectants to shield and soothe the irritated stomach lining.
treatments.name: Anti-nausea Injections and Gastric Protectants (Antacids)
treatments.notes: These medications are crucial for keeping the cat as comfortable as possible while they weather the episode of illness and gastrointestinal distress caused by the mint's volatile oils.
